newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia GDP first post-reform quarterly growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia GDP first post-reform quarterly growth.

text.p: Russia's economy in the first three months of this year recorded its first quarterly growth since the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991, official figures showed on Monday.
But some economists said recent controversial changes in the way the numbers are calculated raised doubts over whether the data gave a true picture of the actual economic situation.
"The great decline in the Russian economy over the last decade has practically ended," Chairman of the State Statistics Committee Yuri Yurkov told a news conference.

Figures released by the committee on Monday showed gross domestic product in the first quarter of 1997 was 0.2 percent higher than a year earlier -- the first growth after seven years of plummeting output.
By the end of last year, the economy was only 61 percent of its size when the Soviet Union broke up and reforms began, returning to levels last seen in 1979.
But some analysts said the figures left much to be desired.

"The Russian economy is a bit blind, it's not clear what total revenues are as well as other key indicators needed to analyse the economy overall," said Vladimir Gurevich, Deputy Editor in Chief of Moscow News.

Critics said the quarterly figures were as suspect as rosy industrial production and GDP figures for the beginning of the year, which were achieved by increasing the weight of the thriving shadow economy, which operates outside the official tax framework, in calculations.
"I refuse to get too excited about it. My impression is that they are over-representing what's going on, said Roland Nash, chief economist at Moscow investment bank Renaissance Capital.
The committee said the shadow economy made up about 23 percent of GDP at the beginning of the year, while earlier calculations gave it a 20 percent weighting.
But it says an upcoming revision of 1996 figures used for comparison will not lead to significant changes in the statistics already published.
Other positive figures published on Monday showed industrial output in March rising 0.4 percent, while year-on-year consumer price inflation slowed to a post-reform low of 16.7 percent.
But GDP in March itself turned down, falling 0.3 percent year-on-year after a 0.1 percent rise in January and a 0.9 percent rise in February.
Yurkov said the positive GDP and industrial production figures did not mean the economy was now growing.
But he said the stable first-quarter GDP was "an incontrovertible fact".
Some economists agreed the underlying trend was stable, although published 1997 growth rates could come down if last year's indicators are revised for the shadow economy.
"I think the numbers support a cautiously optimistic view that we're bouncing along the bottom somewhere," said Vladimir Konovalov, Chief Economist at the World Bank in Moscow.
"Given the fact that it's very difficult to get accurate monthly numbers, the fact that the quarterly numbers are close to zero suggests to me that things are getting better."

Gurevich said the situation could be even better than the official figures show, estimating that the shadow economy accounted for as much as 35 to 40 percent of GDP, as opposed to the 23-25 percent used by the statistics committee.
"These are stable indicators. It's more likely than not that the economy is not shrinking, and there may be growth," he said.
The Russian government has predicted two percent growth this year, but some economists say growth may not resume until 1998.

Earlier this month International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus said Russia could become an economic superpower with annual growth rates of six percent by the turn of the century if it pursued economic reforms.
